title: Should You Tell Students You Like Them
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a colleague's story and an anecdote about a student telling Stuart's daughter that "Mr. Stuart doesn't like me," Stuart argues that teachers should explicitly and directly tell students that they like them. He explains that student motivation runs on signals, and because those signals are invisible to the sender, even well-intentioned teachers can unknowingly transmit "I don't like you" on their harder days. Since students can't reliably intuit the Five Key Beliefs signals a teacher intends, explicit verbal statements of liking, such as "I'm glad you're in my class," close the gap between intention and perception. He frames this practice as a skill to be built through repetition, like an athlete training a muscle, rather than a one-time gesture. The piece is a direct, actionable rapport-building recommendation grounded in his broader Five Key Beliefs framework for student motivation.
points: Stuart's core claim is that because motivational signals are invisible by nature, teachers cannot assume students correctly perceive even well-intentioned Care, so it must be said explicitly.
The anecdote of a student telling Stuart's own daughter "he doesn't like me" is used as concrete evidence that unintentional negative signaling really does reach students.
He offers a specific bank of sayable lines, such as "I'm glad you're in my class" and "I like you," rather than leaving the practice abstract.
Explicitly telling students you like them is framed as a trainable skill, like an athlete practices a sport, not a personality trait some teachers simply have.
quotes: I'm talking about things like this: "Oh, Mr. Stuart? Yeah, he doesn't like me. I talk too much in his class.

The trick with the Five Key Beliefs approach to student motivation is that you can't force students to believe things. All you can do is get really intentional about the signals you're transmitting to them.

Even if you're the most intentional teacher in the world about the signals you're sending to your students, you still don't know if some of your signals might be getting received as "I DON'T LIKE YOU, PUNY STUDENT!!!
And that's why it's so helpful to say sometimes, in a way that makes sense coming from you, things like this: Hey, just so you know — I like you. I think you're great.
And as you're doing it, picture yourself practicing a skill, like an athlete practices a sport. You're gaining muscle. You're building strength.
